5. Keys and relations

Say you add each customer's city to the orders table so finance can sum revenue by city. If one customer appears twice in customers, their orders are counted twice, and the totals stop matching the ledger without anyone being told why. The facts in chapter 4 were about one value at a time: "this column is never NULL", "this one is at least 22". Facts like "one row per order" are of another kind, and two such kinds matter as much in practice:
  • keys: "no two rows have the same id", a fact about pairs of rows;
  • relations between columns: "end is after start", "t1 is exactly one minute after t0", a fact about two values in one row.

Keys with sv.unique

sv.unique("id") says the listed columns identify a row. In requires it is a promise about an input (checked on the data when the input is bound, like any precondition). In ensures it is proved: keys survive filters and projections, and joins whose condition pins down at most one partner on the other side. Joining orders with customers keeps one row per order only if each customer name appears once. We'll try it both ways with the switch:

data.text/markdown:
Other ways to get a key, all proved in SubstraitLean/Keys.lean (Rel.keys_sound):
  • DISTINCT rows are a key: all their columns together;
  • semi and anti joins keep the left side's keys (they only drop rows);
  • a filter x = 3 drops x from a key: unique(id, customer) and customer = 'ada' give unique(id);
  • ROW_NUMBER() with the partition columns is a key (chapter 7).

id any integer or NULL

data.text/markdown:
Relations between columns

Filter and join conditions such as a.t = b.t + 1, start < end or value != -9999 become facts about the row, and they survive projections, joins and unions. Postconditions such as t1 - t0 == 1 or t1 > t0 then follow. Say you prepare training data for a forecasting model. Readings arrive once a minute, -9999 marks a sensor error, and the model needs pairs of consecutive clean readings. Whoever trains it will assume each pair is exactly one minute apart and that no -9999 slipped through, so we'll prove both. The pipeline joins the clean readings with themselves, one minute apart:

data.text/html:
postcondition status
((_.t1 - _.t0) == 1) ✅ proved
(_.t1 > _.t0) ✅ proved
(_.v0 != -9999) ✅ proved
(_.v1 != -9999) ✅ proved
unique(t0) ✅ proved
runtime ⚠️ may wrap around: ($1 + 1)
output column known values
t0 any integer
t1 any integer
v0 any integer
v1 any integer

data.text/markdown:
What each switch does:
  • minute IS NOT NULL: without it, t1 - t0 == 1 is "TRUE or NULL". The join condition w1.minute = w0.minute + 1 is TRUE only for non-NULL values, but Lean only derives that for plain column comparisons, not through the + 1. Lean is conservative: when it can't see a reason, it says so.
  • unique(sensor, minute): one reading per sensor and minute. Within sensor a that makes minute a key, and the join finds at most one t1 per t0, so unique(t0) holds.
  • only sensor a: with several sensors the join pairs readings of different sensors too (there's no sensor in the join condition), so t0 repeats. The relations still hold: they're about each row.
The facts behind these proofs are Expr.factsOf_sound and Rel.facts_sound in SubstraitLean/Contracts.lean: a fact x − y ∈ [lo, hi] or x ≠ k taken from a condition holds on every row that passes it, and is kept by every operator above. Relations that need more than "a column plus a constant" (a < 2 * b) and relations between strings are not tracked yet. You can now prove that a result has one row per key, and that its columns keep the relations the filters and joins set up. Finance's join stays one row per order, and whoever trains the model gets pairs exactly one minute apart, as they assume. Next up: Runtime errors, where a plan that is correct can still crash, or quietly give a wrong number.
